Question: Can you explain the difference between a state vector and a wavefunction in quantum mechanics? Is one more commonly used or preferred over the other?
Answer: These are really the same thing. Both refer to our “representation” for the state of a quantum system when we do the mathematics of quantum theory. Keep in mind that this is just an element of a model we’ve developed. It’s not possible to “see” or measure a wave function in any way. One point of confusion is that this is often presented in a way that implies that the wave function exists as a field in physical space, but that is not correct. Rather, the wave function exists in the “space of possible measurement results” associated with your particular problem. It’s just easy to get confused because often the example that is presented involves the measurement of the position of a single particle, so the space the wave function is in is three dimensional and is isomorphic to physical space. It’s still not really physical space, though. And in other, more complex problems the space may not even be three-dimensional. Stay safe and well! Question: Does the "Measurement Problem" of QM remain in QFT?
Answer: The measurement problem isn’t really a problem. People just expect things from quantum theory that it is not designed to do. Quantum theory is not a theory about what happens in the world in the same way classical theories are. For example, you make a couple of measurements on a golf ball or an artillery shell, and you can grind out its entire future (or past) trajectory - you get a complete picture of “what happened or will happen” in the world. But when you make a measurement in quantum theory you get the result of that measurement, and that is all. Quantum theory is a theory about what we should expect our measurements to be. Consequently, the notions of measurement, observer, instrument, and so on are innately baked into the theory. This bothers some people quite a lot. Tim Maudlin (who also answered this question) comes to mind - he has a particular standard for what a scientific theory should be, and that standard is very much along the lines that it should tell us “what exists,” “what those things that exist do,” and so on. It’s not a bad standard in and of itself, but it’s just not what quantum theory targets. Quantum theory is oriented toward predicting our future perceptions. No less a physicist than the great Richard Feynman counseled us to avoid any assumption about the existence of measurable quantities that we have not actually measured. People agitate a great deal over “what is an observer,” “what constitutes a measurement,” etc. This is a fuzzy thing because it depends on how you set up your problem. Let’s say I have an electron and a Stern Gerlach apparatus. I can certainly regard the electron as a quantum system and the Stern Gerlach apparatus as my “measuring device,” and I can write down my quantum state accordingly. That quantum state will likely say nothing about the apparatus except what its gross state is (say, “ready,” “spin up,” or “spin down.”) With this description in hand, the interaction between the electron and the apparatus is considered a measurement. On the other hand, I can at least imagine regarding the Stern Gerlach apparatus as part of my quantum system. This will require a huge quantum state - that apparatus has a lot of quantum degrees of freedom (many many particles). We can’t actually write that down in practice, but as I said, we can imagine doing so. And then we simply apply Schrodinger’s equation to the whole shebang, and the interaction between the electron and the apparatus no longer represents a measurement in the sense of quantum theory. In a very real way, the “observer” or “measurement” in quantum theory is whatever we decide it’s going to be - it has to do with how we define our quantum state. And if we’re going to get anything useful out of the theory, we must have something in our problem set up cast in the role of observer. Otherwise we never get any probabilities, and that’s the whole point of the business - the prediction of probabilities. Neglecting to properly embrace the flexibility in how the problem setup affects the interpretation of the quantum situation has led to no end of confusion and haggling about things that really don’t represent any sort of profound mystery at all. Question: How did Heisenberg's uncertainty principle contribute to explaining the results of the Double Slit Experiment? Could classical physics alone explain these results?
Answer: The uncertainty principle explains why the waves are perfect plane waves before going through the slits and circular wave front rays after, like this: You see, the waves are explicitly created initially in a way that makes them have a very well-specified momentum. The momentum is purely left-to-right. That means the up-down momentum is zero, and by the uncertainty principle that means that the up-down position is very uncertain. You just don’t know where you’ll find a particular particle along the vertical dimension. But some of the particles go through the slits, and we do know the up/down position of those particles - they have to be lined up with one of the slits. So our up/down position is now tightly specified, and that means the up/down momentum has to be uncertain. Suddenly the particles have an uncertain (and potentially significantly non-zero) up/down momentum. You have some particles going straight on to the right, some going at other angles, and so on - so you get those circular waves. The uncertainty principle really doesn’t play a role in the interference. That just has to do with the fact that different points on the screen are different distances differences from the two slits. Classical physics can explain the interference pattern just fine. The part classical physics has problems explaining is that if you turn the intensity of the light down you start to see individual flashes on the projection screen at random locations. Question: What are the implications and facts that can be derived from the Schrödinger's cat thought experiment?
Answer: That it’s stupid to try to apply quantum concepts to macroscopic situations. One of the assumptions built into quantum theory (which was designed to handle microscopic situations) is that when we make a measurement on a system we will completely replace its quantum state with a new one. The old state affects the probabilities assigned to the possible new states, but it doesn’t affect the actual value of the new state at all. This is just not how classical macroscopic situations work - when we make a classical measurement we may impose a small perturbation on the ensuing physical state, but the previously existing state also has a major effect on the new state. The quantum mechanical process does not allow for this and is therefore inappropriate for application to macroscopic systems. The whole reason Schrodinger published the “cat experiment” to start with was to highlight how wrong it is to try to “think quantum” when dealing with big things like cats etc. A large quantity of the “quantum woo” batted around by the “mystical” crowd in the pop-science media arises from going afoul of this aspect of things. “Is the moon there when no one is looking at it?” Of course it is. The moon is not a quantum system. Ultimately it’s comprised of quantum components, but at the level you interact with it it is thoroughly classical and that’s how you ought to think about it. Question: Did time have a beginning? Do you have evidence for your answer?
Answer: Time is a tricky thing. I think there are two manifestations of time in physics, and you can even see these two flavors in the theory of relativity. On the one hand, you have “coordinate time.” This is the number that we group with spatial coordinates to specify the spacetime coordinates of some event. Coordinate time is really a man-made thing. Spacetime coordinates are just labels within a coordinate system that we set up. There are many, many ways of doing this, and what relativity is basically about is the characterization of “sensible” coordinate systems and how the numerical values of quantities transform depending on what precise coordinate system you view them from. These coordinates are ultimately just as man-made as terrestrial latitude and longitude. And yes, coordinate time has a beginning. You could think of it as a “special point” in the coordinate system much the way the north or south poles are special points in the terrestrial latitude/longitude system (all lines of longitude merge together at those points). Looking backward in time, spacetime “ends” at the Big Bang in a singularity. But - this is not a problem. We can be no more sure that our artificially constructed spacetime “contains all that there is” than we can re: all locations in the universe having a terrestrial latitude / longitude. In fact we are sure about that - we’re sure that the terrestrial latitude / longitude system does not encompass all that there is. There are plenty of places “off Earth’s surface,” and the lat/long system only works on Earth’s surface. Spacetime might turn out to be similarly limited, even though we aren’t aware of any specific things that lie outside of it. I actually think that we have begun to see signs that spacetime is not an all-encompassing “map of reality.” Entanglement related phenomena seem to step outside of it, and so to Einstein-Rosen bridges (wormholes). These are hints to us that “there is more.” Hopefully we’ll gain a better grasp of this in the future. What about the other aspect of time? I said there were two. Well, in relativity you also have “proper time.” This has nothing to do with coordinate time. It’s just the time that will be ticked off by a clock carried with an observer. Each observer has their own personal proper time. Or, rather, each equivalence class of observers that co-move with one another do. The proper time you experience between a pair of spacetime events, if you are present at both of them, depends on the path you follow through spacetime between those events. This is how we get things like the twin “paradox” (quotes there because it’s not really a paradox at all - just something commonly misunderstood). So, I think proper time, or what it represents (time “as experienced”) is a fundamental aspect of reality. On the other hand, coordinate time is artificial and man-made and you shouldn’t get too worked up trying to make something profound out of it. To put these two ideas together, coordinate time ends (along with the spatial dimensions of spacetime) at the Big Bang, but that is no reason for us to assume proper time - time as experienced - ends there. There absolutely could have been something “before the Big Bang” - our coordinate system just doesn’t stretch there. If we ever learn more about that we may require a new coordinate system that does, just as we needed a new three-dimensional coordinate system to map out places off of Earth’s surface. Question: What is the definition of an observer in quantum mechanics? Does consciousness collapse the wavefunction? Does the light needed to see the quantum particle collapse the wavefunction? Is it your eyes that collapse the wavefunction?
Answer: Excellent question. First of all, note that quantum mechanics is not a theory about what happens in the world. Not the way classical physics is. In classical physics you can make a couple of measurements and potentially know how your system is going to behave for the whole future, or how it has behaved for the whole past. You learn about what will happen (or has happened) in the world. Quantum theory doesn’t give this to you. When you make a measurement, you get the result of that measurement, and that is all. Quantum mechanics is a theory about what we should expect to measure in a given situation. This means that observation, observers, measurements, and instruments, and other such things, are “baked into” the theory and you can’t get rid of them. You really can’t set up and solve a problem in quantum theory without specifying your observer. And this brings us to exactly the point. The observer in a quantum mechanics problem is the thing you set the problem up to treat as the observer. This is why there is so much confusion about this. I could regard some laboratory instrument as my observer, set my problem up and solve it, and that would be just fine (so long as I did my work right). But… I could also decide I want to consider that instrument to be part of my quantum system. I could set up a problem like that and solve it, and that would be fine too. It’s the same instrument, but in the first case it does a measurement (it’s an observer), and in the second case it doesn’t. It depends on how I treat it in my problem solving procedure. There does have to be an observer, though, so if I opt to treat my instrument as “part of the quantum system,” then I’ll need something else to server as my observer. The difference between these two cases usually comes down to the level of detail at which I model the instrument in my quantum state. In the second case, where the instrument is part of my quantum system, my quantum system will need to include every quantum degree of freedom of the instrument. For a large lab-size instrument this probably isn’t practical, but we can still imagine doing it. In the first case, where the instrument does an observation, we usually include it in our quantum state only in a very rough way - maybe just enough to capture the different results it can give us. So - the observer is what you decide to treat like an observer when you solve your problem. It’s really that simple. Stay safe and well! Question: Can you explain the concept of "curved spacetime" in physics?
Answer: Yes, but it’s slightly subtle. You probably were exposed to coordinate systems in high school physics. I’m talking about just the plain old x/y or x/y/z (or, if you ever studied relativity, x/y/z/t) coordinate frames. You probably recall that to calculate the distance between two points (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2) you use the Pythagorean theorem: distance = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2) Well, in order for this formula to work, your coordinate system needs to be very regular. We deliberately assign coordinate values to points so that this formula works. But, you can assign those numbers any way you want to, and it is not required that you assign them such that the Pythagorean theorem works. In fact, two points with particular differences in their coordinate values “here” might be a different distance apart from two other points “over there” that have the same coordinate differences. The coordinate values aren’t really 100% arbitrary - scientists usually impose certain “smoothness” requirements on them. But it turns out that in any “good” coordinate system, you can calculate the distance between two points that are very very close together using a slight modification of the Pythagorean theorem. You introduce some “weighting coefficients.” It’s usually written in the form of a matrix. For instance, if your two points are designated by vectors: P1 = transpose(x1, y1, z1) P2 = transpose(x2, y2, z2) (here “transpose” just indicates that I’d really like to be writing these as column vectors) then you can calculate the square of the distance between those points via the matrix / vector expression distance = transpose(P1)*g(x, y, z)*P2 This is a row vector times a matrix times a column vector, and that gives you a number. This matrix g(x, y, z) is called the metric, and its whole purpose is to encode the distances of neighboring points. If you know the matrix g everywhere (it doesn’t have to be the same everywhere), then you can calculate the curvature using various formulas. If you applied these formulas to a flat sheet of paper on a tabletop (regardless of how you had chosen your coordinate system) you’d get zero. But if you calculate the same formula on the surface of a sphere, you’ll get a positive number - the sphere is a surface of positive curvature. All of this is useful because spaces can have different “intrinsic shapes.” A flat sheet of paper is different from the surface of a sphere. On a sphere the angles of a triangle add up to more than 180 degrees. That’s just one example of the differences. We can see this difference by looking at the surfaces embedded in three dimensions but it turns out that you do not need “recourse” to a third dimension to study these things. And in fact our 4D spacetime can be curved, and we don’t need five or more dimensions that we can step out into to see that. Stay safe and well! Question: What are the principles of diffusion?
Answer: Basically that individual (usually microscopic) entities are in random motion. In a container of gas, the molecules are constantly colliding with one another and with the walls of the container, and we are not able to keep up with all of their individual motions, even if we do assume they obey Newton’s simple laws of motion. There are just too many of them for tracking them individually to be practical. Once you have this kind of random motion, if you identify some sub-volume of the region, then at any given time some molecules are moving into that sub-volume from the outside, while others are moving out of it from inside. Both of these processes go on at the same time. Now, assume that for some reason your sub-volume has a higher concentration of gas molecules than the rest of the container. Each individual molecule that’s “inside” has the same probability of crossing to the outside during some interval of time, and each molecule that’s outside has the same probability of crossing to the inside. But - you have a surplus of molecules “inside,” so you will almost certainly wind up with more molecules leaving than coming in. If the concentration in the sub-volume was lower than elsewhere, then you’d almost certainly wind up with more molecules coming in than going out. This is all there is to diffusion - there is just a tendency for things to “even out” as a result of random motion, and this applies to any possible way to distinguish the situation. For instance, if you have oxygen on one side of a barrier and nitrogen on the other side, even at exactly the same temperature and pressure, then when you remove the barrier there will be a tendency for oxygen to flow out of its half and into the nitrogen’s half, and for nitrogen to do the opposite. This will go on until both halves have the same characteristic. It would also apply to regions of different temperature and so on - if you can distinguish a “difference” in the regions, that difference will tend to reduce when you make it possible for the content of the regions to mix. You can make all of this very mathematical using Newton’s laws and the methods of probability theory and statistics, but the concept itself is simple as pie. Hope this helps! Stay safe and well! Question: If the multiverse theory is true, could a parallel world where they’re still in the medieval era and where fantasy elements like magic, dragons, elves, dwarfs is real and common? Parallel world with completely different laws of physics?
Answer: No, not really. Please invest a little time in reading this paper: Here the author sets up an extremely generic model - just a way of describing a universe that could describe any universe imaginable. He doesn’t even assume that space exists initially - time is his only initial independent variable. Then he makes one simple assumption: that in this universe there must be at least one conserved quantity. it doesn’t matter what it is - one just needs to exist. He then extracts the mathematical consequences of this assumption. What you get is basically physics. Our physics. Special relativity, electromagnetism, etc. And you also get space. The number of dimensions the space has isn’t entirely fixed, but he shows that it can’t be just anything. For instance, it can’t be four, or five. Three is allowed, and is in fact the smallest allowed number. I believe the next allowed number is eight, but it’s been a while since I read it. I think if you could pull off the same analysis carrying more terms, you’d get more correct physics. So the upshot is that our laws of physics are more or less required. They are not arbitrary - once you have a conserved quantity, any conserved quantity, you will get a universe very much like ours. Perhaps some of the numerical constants could be different, but the form of the laws of physics is unavoidable. I think this is a profoundly important and very unappreciated paper - it is worth your time trying to slog through it. Stay safe and well! Question: Is light considered more of a particle or a wave? What evidence do scientists use to support their belief?
Answer: Light, like all other “quantum” entities, can manifest either wave like or particle like behavior. Of course, you have no idea what it’s doing unless you make some kind of measurement / observation. Whether you observe wave like or particle like behavior just depends on the details of your experiment and how exactly you are interacting with the light. This isn’t really an “all or nothing” thing - it’s not like light has a “mode switch” that flips it into either “particle behavior” or “wave behavior.” Light just does what it does. The particle or wave attribution comes from how we interpret what we see when we observe the light. If we do Young’s original double slit experiment and see an interference pattern, we think of that as wave like behavior. Then, if we gradually reduce the intensity of the light that pattern begins to become dimmer, and eventually instead of seeing a smooth continuous pattern we’ll begin to see intermittent flashes of light on the display screen, showing up at random intervals. They show up more often where the interference pattern was bright, and less often where it was dim. We think of those individual, very localized flashes as “particle like behavior.” Of course, the original bright interference pattern was made of localized flashes too - there were just so many of them that they blurred together and we couldn’t discern them anymore. So you still have the wavelike behavior of the interference pattern, but along with it you have the particle like behavior of individual localized flashes. You can see both behaviors at the same time. It’s very important to remember than how you engage with the light is critically important to what you observe. The whole point of quantum theory - the big thing that distinguishes it from classical theory, is that in classical theory we tacitly assume that if our technology is good enough then we can reduce the influence we have on the system we’re studying as much as we want to - we can make the “perturbation” we create on the system’s behavior negligibly small if we want to. But quantum theory acknowledges that this is not true - that there is a minimum influence we can have on the system if we interact with it at all, and if that is enough to affect it significantly, then there’s nothing we can do about that. This is probably the most important aspect of quantum theory to understand. Stay safe and well! Question: If I'm on Earth and I push an object upwards, would the force that I exert on the object be present on the object only at the instant when I push it or in a continuous time interval, e.g. between the moment I push and the moment it starts to fall?
Answer: Well, Earth is constantly attracting the object via gravity. So, if you counteract any portion of that force, then… you are exerting some force on the object. The only way for you not to exert any force on it will be if you let it fall in its entirely natural way. Near Earth’s surface the gravitational force is generally regarded as producing a constant acceleration g on the object, directed toward the center of the earth (which we call “down”). So, neglecting air resistance, if the object is not accelerating at g toward the center of Earth, then you must be exerting a force on it. Of course, we’re talking about the vertical direction here - you could exert a force in some other direction. Under normal conditions, the up/down acceleration of gravity is g downward, and the sideways acceleration of gravity is zero. You can apply the same reasoning as above horizontally too - unless the object’s acceleration is g downward and zero sideways, you’re doing something. Stay safe and well! Question: Why does the change in the area of a coil perpendicular to a magnetic field induce an EMF in the coil? Why doesn't this occur in a stationary coil?
Answer: It does occur in a stationary coil. That’s how transformers work - the coils in transformers aren’t moving. What matters is that the total amount of flux passing through the cross sectional area formed by the coil (if it’s a multi-turn coil, then you multiply by the number of turns - the area counts for each one). If that total flux changes with time, a voltage is induced. So, you can cause the flux to change either by changing the field of flux (transformers) or by moving the coil to somewhere there’s a different amount of flux (motors / generators). As far as “why” this relationship exists, well, it just does. Normally when you study electromagnetism from a classical perspective, you just take Maxwell’s equations as given, and one of the terms in Maxwell’s equations captures this relationship. Maxwell wrote the equations the way he did because of the experimental observations we’d made in prior decades. So, we just see that the world behaves this way, that’s all. And then we model it mathematically. Physics tells us how the world behaves, not why it behaves that way. Stay safe and well! Question: What is the scientific explanation for objects emitting light and heat energy without an external source of heat?
Answer: Well, there is a source, long term. An object can emit a photon only if some of the electrons associated with its atoms are in “excited energy states” - that basically means there is some available energy stored inside the object. If one of those electrons falls to its ground state, the energy of the electron drops and that amount of energy is emitted as a photon. So if this is all that happened, then gradually the object would lose all of its available energy - once all of the electrons were in their ground states, there would be no more emission. But that’s not all that’s going on. Random photons flying around in the environment also are absorbed by the object, and that raises new electrons to excited energy levels. All of this is going on all the time - the object is constantly both emitting photons and absorbing photons. Normally the energy rates of the emission and absorption processes will come into balance. If for any reason they are not in balance (say you carry the object into a hot room where there is more loose energy flying around), then the absorption rate will be higher than the emission rate for a while. The amount of energy “in” the object will rise. This is reflected by a rise in its temperature. This increases the emission rate, and that will continue until the emission and absorption rates once again balance. So, if you pay attention to this explanation you see that there is energy balance overall all the time. No energy is just “appearing” or “disappearing.” Stay safe and well! Question: How does general relativity explain the relationship between matter and space? Why does it state that matter bends space instead of the other way around, as described by Newtonian mechanics?
Answer: Newtonian mechanics doesn’t talk about anything “bending” anything. It just calls out a force based on the distribution of matter in the universe. And it’s just an approximation, of course - it turns out that all forms of energy (not just mass) gravitate. Mass is just (far and away) the most dense form of energy we typically encounter - the gravitational effect of energy in other forms is more or less negligible in our day-to-day lives. Also, Newtonian gravity doesn’t propose a mechanism by which this force gets from its source to its target. Newton specifically declined to speculate on that - stating that he would not “pretend to have something to say” about something he didn’t. I think that’s a pretty honorable attitude. You have to understand, these theories say certain things, and they don’t say anything more than that. Newton’s theory described a field of force arising from a field of mass density, with nothing said about how that force traversed space. General relativity describes a field of spacetime curvature (the “metric tensor” of spacetime), arising from a field of energy distribution - with nothing said about why this relationship exists. At least Einstein’s theory has the advantage of being explicitly local, whereas Newton’s theory involves action at a distance. But there is still a relationship proposed that is itself not in any way “explained.” The “why” of it is not addressed. This is typical - generally speaking science is about describing the behavior of nature - not explaining why nature behaves that way. You can use “more fundamental” theories as a “why” explanation for more derivative theories, but ultimately you will reach the “basement level” of the hierarchy and there will be a “why-less” behavior that is simply proposed via some mathematical model. This is because science is an observational endeavor. “Phenomena A behaves this way because phenomena B behaves that way. Phenomena B behaves that way because phenomena C behaves this other way.” Etc. Sooner or later you reach something that just… behaves that way. And we have no idea why. We just look at the world and see that it is so. The best treatment of all of this I’ve seen is this paper: Here, the basement level of the hierarchy is “at least one conserved quantity exists in nature.” From that the paper gets… well, more or less all of low energy physics (low energy only because at one point in the development a Taylor series is truncated and higher order terms are discarded). Even space itself is “derived” here. But… there is no explanation for why at least one conserved quantity must exist. The idea is presented that if not even that held, then there would be nothing but chaos - physics couldn’t even get off the ground. And that feels true to me, but it is hardly an explanation for why a conserved quantity must exist. You might be able to invoke Noether’s theorem (using time translation symmetry - in the paper’s fundamental model time is the only dimension you’ve got, since space isn’t assumed a priori). So the assumption would become “the dynamical relationships are changeless in time.” But then that becomes the “why-less feature.” You can’t get away from having one - a statement is either motivated by some other statement or it is not, and if it is not, it is “why-less.” And we reject circular logic mathematically, so that’s not a way out either. Question: What led Einstein to change his earlier conclusions on the Theory of relativity?
Answer: If you’re talking about the cosmological constant, it is actually a free parameter in the theory. You might think of it as a “constant of integration.” At any rate, Einstein initially set the theory up without it, and then realized that the resulting universe cosmological model was not static. He just assumed that the universe should be static, so he then inserted the constant (or, rather, changed it’s value from zero to non-zero) to force a static universe. Such assumptions not based on observational data are never a good idea, and when the observational data then came a few years later… whoops, the universe was expanding. Einstein then felt that including the constant had been a blunder, so he decided it wasn’t necessary after all. Decades later we discovered that the expansion isn’t just a simple inertial expansion that slows down over time (the “leftovers” of the Big Bang, so to speak), but rather is accelerating. This re-introduced the need for the constant, and we now tune it to get the right rate of expansion. Stay safe and well! Question: Can entangled particles be broken before measuring them at their respective locations? If not, what is the reason for this?
Answer: It’s the measuring that changes the quantum state. Measuring or some “measurement like interaction.” There is a lot of confusion about this, but let me try to help. Let’s say you have a pair of particles that are entangled. Now say one of those has some interaction with another particle. That’s still a very simple quantum system - maybe you now have an entangled system comprised of three particles instead of two. You could still write down a quantum state that described the three particles, and you could still use Schrodinger’s equation to calculate the evolution. If you do that, then this interaction does not represent a measurement. Now consider one of the particles interacting with a laboratory instrument. That’s a whole different thing. You could never write down a fully rigorous quantum state describing that instrument - it has like Avogadro’s number of quantum degrees of freedom. So you can’t apply Schrodinger’s equation. When you do write down a “state” for the instrument, it’s apt to be a very crude state, that captures only the possible outputs of the instrument but does not model all its details. When your entangled particle pair interacts with that, then that is a measurement. It’s a measurement because you are not rigorously modeling the instrument. The only way you can know what state to switch to post-measurement is by looking at the measurement result and then just manually inserting an eigenstate of the instrument operator as the new state. See the difference? “Mesaurement” (of the sort that “causes wave function collapse”) happens when the quantum system interacts with a crudely modeled subsystem. On the other hand, if everything in your problem has been fully modeled, then there’s no problem - you can just apply Schrodinger’s equation and there’s no measurement, no collapse, etc. So this whole “mystery” of “what is a measurement” has a simple answer. What is a measurement depends on how you set up your problem. That’s why the very same subsystem may cause a measurement or may not - it’s just a matter of how you chose to describe that subsystem in your problem setup. Usually it’s clear - “tiny particle can be fully modeled, lab-size instrument can’t.” But there might be cases you run into where you can choose which way you want to go. People cause all kinds of confusion by trying to first think of a lab instrument as a crudely modeled measuring device, and then turn around and think of it as a fully modeled quantum system. But usually in those cases the thing involved can’t be fully modeled for practical reasons. You can imagine doing it, but you can’t really do it. Quantum theory is not a theory about “what happens in the world.” It’s a theory about what we expect to measure. Trying to figure out why it’s not a theory about what happens in the world is a waste of time - it was never intended to be that. Stay safe and well! Question: What are the principles of a laser?
Answer: The goal of a laser is to make as many of the photons produced as possible have precisely the same quantum state. Same frequency, same phase, same polarization, etc. A beam of light that’s as “pure” as possible. Photons are bosons, and that helps out a lot. You may have heard of the Paul Exclusion Principle. That’s the idea that it is impossible to get two fermions to share a common quantum state. Something about their states must be different. Well, bosons are like the opposite. Not only are they not subject to the Pauli principle - they actually have a tendency to fall into common quantum states. So really all you have to do to get a batch of photons to do that is keep them in one another’s proximity for a while. This is what lasers do. A laser is basically a chamber with a fully silvered mirror on one end and a “most” silvered mirror on the other end. Any given photon eventually leaks out through that partially silvered mirror, but on average it bounces around in there for a while first. It’s during this bouncing around that it’s in proximity of a bunch of other photons doing the same thing. During this interval “inside the laser,” they tend toward having a common shared quantum state. That way the ones that eventually leak out are all more or less just alike - just what we want. Of course, you have to have a way to create these photons in the first place, and it helps if you do that in a way that makes photons that all have the same energy. Then the phase and polarization take care of themselves because of all the other photons surrounding them and this “anti-Pauli principle” (there’s no such thing as that - I just said it as a figure of speech). Question: Is the observer effect in quantum mechanics a legitimate phenomena? What about the fact that before observers even existed the universe existed. We come from the universe causally but obsevers are only relatively recent.
Answer: The issue here, fundamentally, is that quantum mechanics isn’t really a theory about “what happens in the world” the same way classical mechanics is. For example, you can solve for the motion of an artillery shell using classical physics and get an entire trajectory. That’s not how quantum mechanics work. Quantum mechanics is a theory about what we expect to measure. The notions of “observer” and “measurement” and “instrument” are baked into the theory in a way that’s just not the case for classical physics. So, the theory is not meant to be applied in the way you’re implying in your question. Unless you actually have an observer and make a measurement, the theory is more or less useless. When you set up a problem in quantum mechanics, you have to decide what your “quantum state” is going to look like. That state will describe the quantum system (a particle, say) you’re studying and will also describe your instrument in some way. There is a difference, though - the description provided for the quantum system is generally fully detailed. You provide a complete description for that. But the instrument probably has something like Avogadro’s number of quantum degrees of freedom (it certainly does if it’s an instrument you can read with your eyes), and you most certainly do not write down a full quantum description of it. So long as your quantum system has not yet become entangled with that instrument, you can apply Schrodinger’s equation to the evolution of the system’s wave function. When you make that measurement, though, the two things do become entangled, and you can no longer apply Schrodinger’s equation because you don’t have a complete description of the system/instrument combination. So, you have to cheat. You look at the instrument and read off the result. Quantum mechanics does not produce your measurement result by some calculation - the measurement result just happens in the world and you look at it. Then if you need to do further problem solving you can modify the state of the system based on your measurement result - that new state doesn’t get “calculated via physics” either. There are people who are very bothered by this failure of quantum theory to be a “theory about what happens in the world” (Tim Maudlin springs to mind). But, it’s the theory we’ve got. I hope this makes sense. Stay safe and well! Kip ____________________ If you enjoy my answers, please consider supporting my work at Kip Ingram's Space.

Question: What is the quantum field theory for someone just starting to learn it?
Answer: It’s a lot of math that’s fairly hard to learn, for one thing. Conceptually it’s not that awful - the basic process you go through is that you know what your “initial conditions” are (the particles you have coming in toward a potential interaction). You then basically guess at possible final configurations (particles created, annihilated, etc., and how they are behaving), and then you can calculate the probability of the initial config leading to that final config. You repeat this process for more guessed final configs, until the total probability you have accounted for so far gets close enough to 1.0 to suit you. If it’s well below 1.0, then there’s some final configuration you haven’t considered yet. That’s basically it. The math takes care of enforcing conservation laws and all other physical requirements. The big difference between this and classical physics is that you do not “calculate” the final configuration - you “propose it” (guess at it) and then see how likely that is. I assume that with experience you get better and knowing what final configs to consider. Stay safe and well! Question: What are the odds of getting a royal flush without jokers in a standard deck of cards?

Question: What is the reason for most containers being shaped as cylinders instead of other shapes like rectangles, squares, triangles, pentagons, or hexagons?
Answer: Cylinders are stronger. Also, circles, spheres, and so on (depending on the number of dimensions you’re working in) contain the largest amount of “inside” for the given amount of “outside.” For example, a circle encloses more area than any other shape you can make with a perimeter of that length. So, a square encloses less area than a circle, the perimeters being equal. Say you pump compressed gas into a square bottle. That internal pressure will push out on the side walls, and because a circle has greater area than a square (perimeters equal), there will be a tendency for the bottle to deform unless you make the walls really thick and strong. Question: How do rockets maintain flight without wheels? What prevents them from crashing upon landing?
Answer: Rockets are the simplest, most physically “direct” form of keeping things off the grown. They get momentum in their “forward” direction, whatever it is, by hurling mass out the back in the other direction. Momentum is conserved. Force is the time derivative of momentum, so by playing this momentum game (mass of exhaust times velocity of exhaust), the rocket can produce an “forward” force on itself. If “forward” is “up,” then the right amount of that can offset the downward force of gravity. Nothing could be simpler. So, in order to “not crash,” the rocket just has to keep itself pointed precisely upward (so the force is in the right direction), and burn the right amount of fuel per second. Getting all that just right isn’t particularly easy, and historically rockets did usually crash when they were done doing their main mission. Recently, though, precision electronic control has become good enough to allow rockets to gracefully land, upright, on a landing pad. Question: Is it theoretically possible to travel faster than the speed of light inside a spaceship while staying within its hull limits?
Answer: No. The idea here is that the relative speed between any two things you choose to use for your speed determination must be less than the speed of light. For example - say Bob passes Alice as some speed v1. That speed v1 must be less than c. At the same time, Charlie passes Bob (same direction) at some other speed v2. That speed v2 must be less than the speed of light. Now, that means that Charlie passes Alice at some other speed, v3. Well, v3 must be less than the speed of light too. Even if v1 = v2 = 0.999*c, v3 will still be less than c. This is one of the very non-intuitive things about relativity, but it is nonetheless true. So, in your question, your spaceship must be traveling less than c relative to Earth. You must be traveling less than c relative to your spaceship, and you must be traveling less than c relative to Earth. The way velocity “compose” (the way you get the v3 above if you know v1 and v2) is such that you can never wind up with a result bigger than c, as long as the two input velocities are less than c. It’s a rather remarkable fact that the math of special relativity is 100% internally self-consistent; you can’t concoct any situation that will let you squeak around this limitation. Question: Is it possible to fully understand why particles behave a certain way after a measurement is made in quantum mechanics experiments?
Answer: To talk about particles “behaving in a certain way” after a measurement implies that you make further measurements to assess that behavior. That’s a more complicated thing that you should be talking about. Instead you should ask “is it possible to fully understand why particles have a particular quantum state after a measurement is made in quantum mechanics experiments?” Because these are the two things that a measurement brings about. First, you get a result for the measurement - a number, and second you get a new quantum state for the particle after getting that result from the measurement. The program of basic quantum mechanics does not tell you what your measurement result is going to be. It may give you a collection of possible results, but it depends on the particular situation - that “collection” may be “all possible results.” It also gives you the probability that you will get each of those possible results. But the result itself “just happens,” and you have to actually look at your instrument output to know for sure what it is. Once you do know the result, the post-measurement quantum state is indeed specified - in the general case there is a one-to-one correspondence between “the result” and the “post measurement state.” So as soon as you look at that result, you also know the new state to associate with the particle. And the only justification we have for this, in the context of the theory, is “because the theory tells us so .” Basic quantum mechanics is not a physical theory about what happens in the world. It is a prescription that tells us what to expect from our future measurements. We are not able to directly measure a quantum state, so we can’t “check the state” after the measurement to confirm it is what we’ve said it is. All we know is that if we assume that is the post-measurement state, further predictions that we make tend to turn out right. So, if you want to get a more clear perspective on what quantum theory is all about, stop talking about “what happens in the world.” Stop talking about fuzzy things like “the behavior of a particle.” Talk instead about measurement results, because that is really all that the theory addresses. Everything else is just part of a model we’ve built. Stay safe and well! Kip ____________________ If you enjoy my answers, please consider supporting my work at Kip Ingram's Space.

And no matter how you try to handle that, it will eventually boil down to a round-trip light beam being required to do that synchronization. You can dress it up and make it more and more complicated, but at the bottom of it all there is always a round trip. So no, we can’t truly measure the one way speed of light - only the two way speed of light. We assume that space time is homogeneous (no special places, no special times) and isotropic (no special directions). So given that assumption there is no reason to suppose that light would travel at different speeds in different directions. The rational assumption is that direction doesn’t matter, and so you can get the speed of light just fine from a round-trip measurement. Question: If two identical twins were separated and one went into a black hole, would they be different when they reunited? How does time dilation affect them in this scenario?

The parameter m0 is the initial total mass of the vehicle, including its structure, its fuel, and its payload - everything. The parameter mf is the final mass, generally the initial mass minus the fuel. This equation places limits on what a single stage can accomplish. After you’ve burned a bunch of your fuel, a single-stage vehicle still has to carry all the mass it took to contain that fuel, so further delta-v it gets from there has to include that mass in the new m0. You can get much better benefit from your “later fuel” if you get rid of the mass you needed to contain the fuel you already burned. Hence multiple-stage rockets make a lot of sense - they allow the last fuel you burn to do get you a lot more delta-v than it otherwise would. So, you see, this isn’t just something someone thought was cute. There is a very sound and rational mathematical reason why it makes sense. We likely wouldn’t have been able to do moon missions in the 1960’s had it not been for multi-stage techniques. Stay safe and well! Question: Is the concept of time slowing down and length contracting true when traveling at high speeds? Can an object ever reach the speed of light?
Answer: Yes, it’s true - it has been experimentally verified. However, it’s important to understand exactly what we’re talking about here. Nothing about the object being observed actually changes. For example, if you were moving at high speed and I was observing you, you would not feel anything at all unusual about how time was passing for you or your length in various directions, etc. These are things that I would perceive when I observed you. It’s all about that “observation process” - that’s where the changes all come in. Nothing happens to the moving object, because you can’t even say in a valid way that “it’s moving.” You’re perfectly free to regard it as sitting still and the things around it as moving. No, nothing that has mass can reach the speed of light. The easiest way to grok this is to consider that when you make an object move you must cause it to have kinetic energy. In your high school physics this is written as 0.5*m*v^2, but that is only a “low speed” approximation. The correct expression, even at high speeds is this: Kinetic Energy = m*c^2*[ 1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2) - 1] If you look at how that behaves as an object moves closer and closer to the speed of light, you’ll see that it rises without limit toward infinity. If you try to plug in v = c, it becomes literally infinite. So, the restriction is that there is no way for you to give an object infinite kinetic energy. No matter how much energy you give it, all you’ll get for it is “closer to the speed of light” - you never get there. Then there are particles that have no mass. They still need to be able to carry energy and momentum, and using the above formula that tells you right away that they can’t travel at any speed less than the speed of light. If you give them such a speed and run the energy formula above, you get zero energy, because of zero mass. If you give them speed c, though, you get zero divided by zero, which is undefined. Meaning the expression just doesn’t tell you anything about the energy of the particle - it could be anything. And, in fact, it is equal to Planck’s constant h multiplied by the particle’s frequency. Question: What is the twin paradox and how did Einstein use math to solve it? Is it possible to observe this phenomenon in real life?
Answer: First of all, it’s not actually a “paradox.” People just think it is when they think about special relativity the wrong way. We live our lives at very low speeds - tiny speeds compared to the speed of light. As far as relativistic effects are concerned, we may as well all be sitting still relative to one another. When we are stationary relative to others, then our “flow of time” matches there’s precisely - we can all wear accurate wristwatches and they’ll always agree. We do move around relative to one another, and that does cause these wristwatches to tick off slightly different amounts of time in between our meetings with one another. But given the speeds we move around at, those effects are far to small to detect unless you are using very sophisticated clocks. On the other hand, if we moved around during out days at relative velocities significant compared to the speed of light, we’d consider it routine for us to meet up and find our clocks don’t agree. Alice and Bob can both be together at breakfast, and they can sync up their watches. But then if Bob goes and flies around doing things, at speeds large compared to the speed of light, then when he meets back up with Alice at dinner they’ll find that Bob’s watch is lagging behind Alices. That is just the most simple and straightforward application of the equations of relativity. It is trivial to show that it will be the case, and experiments have confirmed this effect. Where people get confused though, is that they say to themselves, “But wait a minute. Doesn’t relativity say that I can regard Bob has having been stationary and Alice as having moved around? And, if so, then how can one of them have less time pass?” Well, no, you can’t do that. It is not the case that Alice and Bob have had symmetrical experiences. In order to move away from Alice at something like the speed of light and then return to meet her again, Bob has to follow a path that includes periods of acceleration. Alice can just sit still all day. So they did not have the same experiences - Bob accelerated, Alice didn’t. It’s not the acceleration per se that causes the differential aging effect, but the acceleration is required in order to execute the motions through spacetime that do cause it. If you were to really make Bob and Alice symmetrical - if you were to have them both accelerate away from each other, at equal rates, and then later they both turn around and come back together, having equal magnitude accelerations at all times, then you would find that they were the same age. That would be a symmetrical situation. Stay safe and well! Kip ____________________ If you enjoy my answers, please consider supporting my work at Kip Ingram's Space.

Question: If J C Maxwell had not come up with his electro-magnetic equations in the 1860's is there anyone else who could have before 1900?
Answer: That is a very hard question to answer reliably. Work in electricity and magnetism had been ongoing for decades. Faraday, Ampere, etc. The experimental data was appearing, and the connection between electricity and magnetism was noticed - that all happened without Maxwell being necessary. In particular, Faraday’s work introduced the notion of fields that filled space to the study. What Maxwell brought to the table was a particularly mathematical mind. His whole project began with the goal of taking Faraday’s and Ampere’s work and placing it into a rigorous modern mathematical form. His training was right for this - he held the mathematical tools at his command. His work was almost straightforward, given his background. In the end, though, he looked at the result and recognized that it was flawed. There was a mathematical inconsistency in it, even after all of the known experimental phenomena had been properly inserted. Maxwell corrected this situation by adding a term to one of the equations. Here are Maxwell’s equations (in their modern form - Maxwell himself didn’t write them anything like this elegantly): In the last equation, Maxwell added the last term. It had never been noticed in earlier work because that factor 1/c^2 is a very, very small number. But the addition corrected the problems, and when Maxwell then studied those equations he recognized that propagating electromagnetic waves should exist. He calculated the speed they should propagate at, and recognized that value as the (already known) speed of light. This made him realize that light is simply a form of EM radiation, and that many other sorts of “light,” differing from visible light only by frequency, should exist. And that unlocked the door to radio, television, and all of the other applications of electromagnetic waves that form the basis of our technological culture today. It opened the way to a better understanding of issues plaguing ocean-floor telegraph cables, etc. Would someone else have done this by 1900? As I said, it’s very hard to say. I want to think “probably.” None of the steps Maxwell took were unimaginably inspired - they were things that you’d expect any properly competent (mathematically competent) person working in the field might have seen. So I think yes, but who knows? It might have taken decades longer. You should keep in mind that special relativity became necessary because Maxwell’s equations were fundamentally at odds with Newtonian mechanics. Everyone expected it would be Maxwell’s equations that “had to give,” but it wasn’t - when Einstein brought forth special relativity it was Newton’s mechanics that he modified. Also, the necessity for quantum mechanics arose out of the study of black body radiation, and Maxwell’s equations were necessary to make that necessity evident. So, if Maxwell’s equations had come later, a whole lot of other things would have come later too. Nuclear energy research would likely have been postponed, and World War II would have had an altogether different ending. So the alternative history you are asking about would have indeed been a very different one. Stay safe and well! Question: When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet?
Answer: We never directly observe a particle. We get a result from an instrument that we claim has something to do with the particle. What you need to remember here is that basic quantum mechanics is not a theory about “what’s happening in the world.” It’s a theory about how we expect our future measurements to behave. That means that the notions of measurement, observers, and instruments are inextricably embedded in the theory, which is something you don’t really want in a “theory about the world.” The bottom line is that before you make your measurement, you don’t know what the result is going to be. There is natural non-determinism in the world, and therefore all we can hope for is to know the set of values that result might have and the probability of each one. Basic quantum mechanics gives us a way to ascertain these things, and the multi-valued nature of the future result possibilities is represented by an “uncollapsed wave function.” This wave function does not exist in physical space (sometimes the dimension is not even right). It exists in a “space of possible measurement outcomes.” Treating it as though it’s an entity in physical space will lead to confusion. Now, when you do make the measurement, you can look at the results and now you know what it is. Note that the theory does not contain any physics that captures this change. Now that we know the value, the previous wave function which allows for many outcome possibilities no longer makes any sense. So the methodology instructs us to replace it with one that is restricted to that single outcome possibility. The wave function in possible measurement outcome space collapses to that single realized value. Nothing whatsoever has happened in physical space, so no consideration of whether it happened “faster than light” or not makes any sense at all. Now, what if the possible results formed a continuous range, and you can’t read a precise value off of your instrument, but only a “really good approximate value”? Well, if you wanted to be pedantic you would not replace the wave function with a Dirac delta on “the result.” You’d replace it with a new wave function that captured your uncertainty in reading the instrument. That’s what would put you in the best position going forward toward further evolution and measurements. A lot of people don’t like it at all that quantum mechanics has this “measurement centric” nature - they want a theory that simply describes the physical world, independent of anything we’re doing to look at it. But that’s just not the theory we’ve got. It’s not really fair to criticize the theory because of this - it was designed to be this way, and within its designed arena it is a fantastic and wildly accurate and useful theory. If you want the other kind of theory, well, go try to find it - everyone would be happy if you came up with it. Stay safe and well! Question: Why is the speed of light considered the ultimate speed limit in the universe? How is this concept tested experimentally, and are there conditions under which particles can travel faster than light?
Answer: One of the things we learned by just looking at the world is that steady motion has no effect on the laws of physics. That is, if you are sealed up in a lab and can gain no information about the outside world, there is no experiment you can do that will tell you whether your lab is “sitting still” vs. “moving at a high but unchanging velocity.” It’s a good thing this is true, because we’re all zipping along at quite a high rate of speed due to Earth’s motion in the solar system. It can be show with fairly straightforward math (that is, a bright high school kid could follow the reasoning and analysis) that if you want to demand that the laws of physics have this invariance under constant velocity motion, then there must be a “special speed” - if I measure an object to be moving at this speed, then all other observers will also measure it moving at that same exact speed, regardless of whether we’re all moving with respect to one another or not. This is very counter to our intuitions, but it’s a requirement if you want that invariance. We can (arbitrarily) use the letter c to denote this speed. Further straightforward math shows that the formulas we learn in high school for kinetic energy and momentum: Energy = m*v^2/2 Momentum = m*v are just approximations that hold only when the velocity v is “much less” than the special speed c. It turns out the correct formulas are Energy = m*c^2*[1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2) - 1] Momentum = m*v/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2) If you look closely at that energy expression, you will see that no matter how much kinetic energy you pour into an object, you can never get its velocity up to c. The energy rises toward infinity as the velocity approaches c. This is all it takes to make c an upper bound on velocity - nothing can ever have an infinite amount of energy associated with it. The expression further says that if a particle has zero mass, then at all velocities less than c its energy will be zero However, if you try to set v = c, the expression goes to 0 / 0, which is undefined. So the formula says nothing about the energy of a zero mass particle moving at the speed c. It turns out that massless particles must move at this speed in order to carry any energy or momentum, and that’s the behavior of photons. So, massive things must move slower than c, and massless things must move at c. Note that none of this has told us what c’s value is. That turns out to be something we have to measure - there’s no way to “derive” it from theoretical considerations alone. Numerous attempts were made in the late 1800s to use Earth’s motion to let us catch light moving at different speeds in different directions. They all failed. These were good experiments, and absolutely should have worked, if indeed light did move at different speeds in different directions. So, the only rational conclusion is that it does not do that - it always moves at c regardless. Stay safe and well! Question: Is it possible to create a laser beam or something similar using only one mirror and without using any lenses?
Answer: Laser light is a very special kind of light. There are a number of parameters that characterize a photon - you have frequency, phase, and polarization, nominally. In a normal light source you have a whole bunch of photons and they all tend do have different values for these parameters. It’s just a mixed up mess. Laser light, however, is characterized by photons that mostly all have the same frequency, the same phase, and the same polarization. We call this “coherent light.” Essentially, we get most of the photons (all of them, ideally) into a single shared quantum state. We’re able to do this because photons are bosons, which mean they have interger quantum spin rather than half-energy quantum spin (fermions, like electrons). Fermions are subject to the Pauli exclusion principle, which means you can’t even have two fermions that have a fully shared quantum state, much less an extremely large number of them. But, in contrast, bosons actually “like” to get into a shared state. If you just get a bunch of photons together for a period of time, they will tend toward a uniform state. Lasers work by doing exactly this. Photons are generated in a chamber that has mirrors on both ends. One of the mirrors is partially silvered, so that photons most likely bounce but sometimes pass through. So the beam is formed of the photons that leak through the mirror, but in general they have bounced around in there for a while first, and that gives them the opportunity to find that common quantum state. So it’s a pretty simple idea - the devil is in the details, of generating the photons in the first place, making sure those mirrors are nice and parallel, and so on. Stay safe and well! Question: Can matter undergo continuous phase transitions?

Question: Could entropy be seen as the will towards disorder and chaos?
Answer: No, not really. Entropy really just arises out of randomness. In any system of that sort, there is generally a truly gargantuan number of configurations that the system could exist in, even after you’ve satisfied constraints like conservation of energy, momentum, and so on. For example, consider a container of gas molecules that has a certain energy E, and assume that it’s isolated from the environment so no energy can enter or leave. That means the total kinetic energy of all the molecules has to add up to E, at all times. But you could accomplish that in an enormous number of different ways. The system is constantly moving around among these ways just due to the occasional collisions between gas molecules. One assumption of thermodynamics is that none of these possible configurations are “special” - the system is as likely to be in any one of them as it is any other. That said, we can still categorize those configurations in various ways. For instance, there is a category of possible configurations where all of the energy E is possessed by just one molecule. If there are N molecules, then there are N configurations that fall into this category. Or we could have all of the energy in just two molecules, evenly divided. There are N*(N-1) ways of getting this. For three molecules, it would be N*(N-1)*(N-2) configurations. Notice that we haven’t even discussed uneven divisions of the energy among our molecules, and that’s a way of varying configurations too. Anyway, the upshot of this is that there are many, many, many more possible configurations that have the energy smeared out over a lot of molecules than there are ways of having it all in just a few molecules, and since all of these configurations are equally likely it’s almost certain you’ll find the energy all smeared out. In fact, you can predict a precise speed distribution - it’s called the Boltzmann distribution and that’s the state a gas will tend to. So there is no “will” in this - it’s really just the mathematics of random variation. An easy way to play with this idea is to just shuffle a deck of cards. It’s possible that you might shuffle the deck into a state that has all of the red and black cards separated from one another. But, there are 52! ways you can arrange that deck of cards, and of those only 2*(26!)^2 are “separated” arrangements. If you work that out it tells you that the probability of shuffling into separation is only about 4e-15. Starting from a separated state, shuffling will drive you away from separation as a matter of pure random chance. Stay safe and well! Question: How do I start learning polynomials and matrix? I know what is field and ring, complex numbers, etc. What books do you suggest?
Answer: There are many good books, and the present the material in different ways - one of those ways will work best for you, and that’s the one for you. But you almost don’t even need a book - all of this stuff is “out there” online these days, and you can get at all of it for free. Matrices connect most closely with the branch of math called linear algebra. I’ll try to give you a quick sketch, just so you have a vague feel for it. This is not a thorough coverage in any way. We’ll use two variables, just to keep things simple, but all the same ideas apply to any number of variables. Say your variables are x and y. You can think of them together, like this: [ x, y ]. That is a vector. If we had three variables, it might be [ x, y, z ]. For larger variable counts, people often write it like this instead: [ x1, x2, x3, … xn ]. But we’ll stick with two. Each item in a vector is called a component. Now consider a linear function of your vector’s components: a*x + b*y. This will of course just be a number. Notice that we have two components, x and y, and there are also two coefficients, a and b. So the list of coefficients behaves an awful lot like a vector too, but it is subtly different and is sometimes called a “covector.” If the vector is V and the covector is C, then you could think of that linear function as the product of a covector and a vector: C*V. Often vectors are written in column form, with x, y, and so on going from the top down, and covectors are written in row form, the way we wrote it left to right above. Now a matrix is just a group of components that has more than one row and more than one column. You can think of it as a vertical stack of covectors, one on top of another, or a horizontal “stack” of vectors, all arranged beside one another. You can think of these rows and columns of numbers as representing points in some sort of space. If a vector denotes a point in a space, then a covector denotes a point in a “dual space.” These are different but related spaces. If I just hand you one of these points, how do you get components associated with it? To do that, you have to choose a coordinate system. In two dimensions that would mean choosing a unit vector to be your x axis and another unit vector at 90 degrees to the first one to be your y axis. That choice associates a pair of numbers with every point in the space and in the dual space. Note that if you change those axes - say you rotate them, that changes the components, but you’re still talking about the same point. I won’t try to go any further with that - hopefully it gives you a small taste. Linear algebra is the formal study of these vectors, covectors, and how they transform around under changes of coordinate system. Polynomials are similar, but instead of having multiple variables you have multiple powers of one variable. Instead of x and y you would have x^0 (which is 1) and x. Instead of x, y, and z, you’d have x^0 (1), x, and x^2. As you go to higher dimension you just run that power right on up. I do want to recommend one book to you - this book should help you “get your bearings,” and help you figure out the areas you need to do more work in. It’s sort of a “broad overview” of the important math. It’s called All The Math You Missed (But Need to Know for Graduate School) and was written by Thomas Garrity. Good luck! Stay safe and well! Question: In quantum entanglement how can one actually “prove” that the first measurement on the first particle is purely random and uncorrelated to something else unknown to the observer?
Answer: The general procedure would be to conduct an ensemble of experiments. Prepare the system the same way ever time and repeat the measurement a large number of times. And then show that there is no correlation between the result and whatever other factor you are concerned about. Determining the correlation between a pair of data sets is just a math calculation, so this is straightforward. This whole procedure is predicated on the idea that the quantum state is a complete specification of the state of a system, because “preparation” means “getting the system into a particular quantum state.” It is wrong to think of the first measurement as random and the second as somehow “caused” by the first outcome. There is no causal connection between the two events. Rather, the pair of outcomes are random, but related. It’s a bit like flipping a coin and noting that the face that is up is always the opposite of the face that is down. Of course it is, but we don’t say that “heads being up” causes tails to be down or vice-versa. Those are just related conditions, and they both either occur or don’t occur together. The fact that there can be a time difference between the measurements in the entanglement case doesn’t change this. After all, the whole point of the entangled state is that it stipulates this relationship - you don’t know until one of the measurements is made what the outcomes of the measurements will be, but you know from the minute the state is created that the particular entangled relationship holds. Question: How much slower is half the speed of light compared to the actual speed of light? Is there a non-mathematical way to determine this?
Answer: It’s half. The speed of light is 3e8 meters/sec; half the speed of light is 1.5e8 meters per second. With just one observer and one moving object involved, that’s all there is to it. You may be wondering about how velocities compound when multiple observers themselves in relative motion are involved. Let’s say Alice sees Bob go by at half the speed of light. Then Bob sees an object pass him, in the same direction, at half the speed of light. One might naively thing that Alice would see that object moving at the speed of light (half plus half is one, right?), but that’s not the case. The formula for compounding velocities like that is this: v = (v1 + v2) / (1 + v1*v2/c^2) We can let c = 1 and solve our problem above like this: v = (0.5 + 0.5) / (1 + 0.5*0.5) = 0.8 So Alice would see the object pass her at 80% of the speed of light. If Bob saw the object go by at the full speed of light, then Alice would too: v = (0.5 + 1.0) / (1 + 0.5*1.0) = 1.0 The way the velocity addition law was figured out in the first place was by demanding that if an object moves at c for one observer, it must move at c for all observers. If there is only one observer, though, and two moving objects, then half of a velocity is just the plain old half of the velocity. Stay safe and well! Question: Can you explain the concept of "the fine-tuning of the universe" and provide an example of something that is considered to be finely tuned?
Answer: In the Standard Model, there are a couple of dozen numerical “parameters” that the theory doesn’t nail down a value for - that is, there’s no way to determine from the theory alone what these parameters “need” to be. We have to measure them experimentally, which we have done, and using those values the theory gives us good predictions. As far as we can tell, there is no particular reason why these parameters must have the particular values they have - if there were such reasons, then we’d be able to derive values theoretically. So we can’t explain why they are these value instead of some other values. What we’ve discovered, though, is that it looks like if some of these parameters had turned out to be different, even by a percent or two in some cases, higher or lower, then for various reasons it’s highly unlikely that the universe would be suitable for life. For example, the fine structure constant has to do with the strength of the electromagnetic interaction (how hard charges pull and push on each other). If you moved that value a few percent one way or another, then chemistry just wouldn’t work, and we couldn’t be here. There are numerous cases like this, and “the fine tuning problem” is the need to explain “how we got so lucky,” so to speak - how it came to be that these values turned out “just right” for us to exist. One explanation people put forward is multiverse theory. In that model, there is a huge number of universes, and the parameters just turn out kind of random in each one. So you’re bound to find a few here and there that are good for life. That does indeed solve the problem, but on the other hand we really have zero evidence at all as to the existence of other universes and there is really no hope of ever having such evidence, so the idea is “non-falsifiable” and that’s bad in scientific thinking. My favored solution is to just take an idealism-based view of reality. There are two broad ways of looking at things - materialism and idealism. Materialism posits that the physical world is the fundamental reality, and that our minds arise out of physical processes in some manner. The problem is that no one has been able to even start to clearly state what that “some manner” is - no one has a model for conscious thought that even gets off the ground. Idealism, on the other hand posits that “mind” is fundamental, and what we label the physical world is just the perceptions of our minds. Materialists will try to make you think that idealism is tantamount to mysticism, but it’s really not - the truth is that in science all we have is our perceptions, and science has absolutely nothing to say about how those perceptions make their way to us. That’s just a closed book that we can’t look into. However, if you give an idealism-based model a little thought, you’ll see that the fine tuning problem just goes away. Minds exist as an initial postulate - a given. And then those minds go and try to make models of their perceptions, so they can predict what their future perceptions will be. That’s science. And of course the perceived reality will have to turn out to be one that supports the existence of minds, since minds are in fact there as the initial assumption. A model that appeared to prohibit the existence of life altogether would just be an inconsistent model, since we are in fact here. So, you have to decide for yourself what you think of those positions. Science really can’t make that determination for you. I rather doubt it will ever be able to, but it’s always dangerous to depart from the “never say never” attitude. Stay safe and well!
