Question: How can light have momentum without having mass? Why does it not follow Newton's laws of motion?
Answer: Momentum is a more sophisticated idea than you were taught in high school physics. Most early physics training starts right off with “momentum is mass times velocity,” and says little more about it, until they start just introducing these exceptions, like the momentum of light. And they never really explain that to any great depth - you’re just given a separate formula for the momentum of photons - Planck’s constant divided by the de Broglie wavelength. When you get to a more sophisticated level you learn how to use the mathematical concept of group theory to get greater insight into physics. In group theory there are these things called “generators.” A generator is basically an “infinitesimal transformation” in the space the group lives in. Even an infinite group can have a finite number of independent generators. For example, all possible 3D rotations from a group - an infinite one - but there are only three generators, which you can think of as infinitesimal rotations around each of the three axes x, y, and z. Any rotation can be produced through a suitable infinite sequence of these infinitesimal rotations. A lot can be learned about a group form its generators. Anyway, in physics it turns out that momentum is the “generator” of spatial translation. Loosely speaking, this means that any physical entity that moves through space must have momentum. It doesn’t matter whether it has mass or not - if it moves, it has momentum. It just so happens that for a particle with mass that momentum is equal to mass times velocity - that’s handy, but it’s not the “core profound meaning” of what momentum is. Light moves through space. Therefore it has momentum. There is no mass, so the mass times velocity formula is useless. This makes even more sense if you look at the relativistic formula for momentum that m*v is the low-speed limit of: p = m*v / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) For a photon, the numerator of this fraction is zero, because mass is zero. But the denominator is zero too, because you have to plug in v = c, and you wind up taking the square root of 0. So this expression winds up being zero divided by zero, which is undefined. That means that it doesn’t nail down the momentum at all - it still could be anything, and in fact that’s exactly right - the actual momentum depends on the wavelength. Question: If momentum= velocity*mass than according to the formula light momentum will be zero but light have momentum ‘, light mass is zero?
Answer: This is a common question. The answer is that it’s simply not true that momentum is only mass times velocity. That’s how you’re taught in high school physics, but that teaching is incomplete. Momentum is the “generator” of spatial translation. That terminology comes from the application of group theory to physics. Basically, what it means is that anything - anything whatsoever - that moves through space must have non-zero momentum in order to do so. Anything that has zero momentum is sitting still. Please do remember that whether or not something is sitting still depends on your choice of coordinate system, so all of this is observer dependent to some degree. But, light moves through space, so you expect it to have momentum, based on that way of looking at it. The same type of reasoning applies to energy. Energy is the generator of time translation - anything that “moves through time” (i.e., exists / persists in time) must have energy associated with it. If something truly had zero energy, it could not persist in time and we’d be wholly unable to detect it - there is no place in our physics for things we can’t detect and that have no effect on anything we can detect. Obviously, you can’t use the formula mass times velocity to determine the momentum of a photon of light, since it has no mass. Instead, you calculate its momentum as Planck’s constant h divided by the wavelength of the photon. So, that’s all there is to it - your assumption that momentum implies mass is just incorrect. Question: What is the origin of the concept of infinity? How did humans discover the idea of something never-ending despite being limited by time and space?
Answer: We invented numbers. And, eventually, we got hold of the Hindu-Arabic numeral system for designating them. This system never ends. So, for the first time, we had access to a “mechanism” so to speak - a mental-only one, but still - that could support the notion of a never-ending sequence. After that it was just a matter of time. Arithmetic helped. We learned to add subtract, multiply, and - most importantly - divide. It was immediately clear that there was something “wrong” with dividing by zero, but eventually we started looking at the idea of dividing by a number ∊ and letting ∊ approach zero. No matter how close we got, it was still a valid arithmetic operation, but the result just went up and up and up. So, you can see that there were a number of “avenues” to infinity in our system of numbers and arithmetic - eventually someone just decided to look specifically at that idea. Then there was Cantor, who recognized that there are “degrees” of infinity - the infinity of the real numbers, or even just the real numbers between zero and one, is infinitely larger than the infinity of the integers. This can be shown rigorously. Eventually the study of infinity got quite sophisticated. To some extent this is what mathematicians do - they take anything that can be studied, and they study it in the most sophisticated way possible. And it’s amazing how often those things wind up being useful somehow, say in science. A lot of folks make jokes about mathematicians, but I’m awfully glad they’re there. Stay safe and well! Question: Given 3 spaceships A, B, C, with B moving faster than A, and C moving faster than B, with clocks on each. If B shows time dilation relative to A, and C shows time dilation relative to B, what will be the time dilation experienced by C relative to A?
Answer: Well, the easiest thing to do would be just to calculate the A/C time dilation directly. You know all the relative velocities. There is a formula for compounding velocities - basically if you know the velocity of B as far as A is concerned and the velocity of C as far as B is concerned, then you can compound them to get the velocity of C as far as A is concerned. Even if A/B and B/C are 99% of the speed of light, A/C will still be less than the speed of light. That’s just how it works. I don’t know a time dilation compounding formula offhand, but it likely wouldn’t be that hard to derive one. Question: What is the reason for our universe existing in three dimensional spacetime instead of one dimensional time or two dimensional spacetime? Could it have existed in a different dimensional space?
Answer: Excellent question. Please let me refer you to this paper by Christian Baumgarten: I will try to summarize it for you; you really need to wade through it to “see” it mathematically, but I can at least tell you what the conclusions are. Baumgarten sets up a generic approach to modeling “any universe.” His basic model is just an arbitrarily large collection of functions of time (only). There is no presumption of any spatial dimensions whatsoever. If you give this some thought, you should agree that if I handed you the full history of any imaginable universe (any number of spatial dimensions, any set of physical laws, etc. etc.) you could write down that history in this “Baumgarten form.” So, it’s important to emphasize that at this initial point we have no space - we are not “taking it as a given” as is normally done in general discussions of physics. Most treatments start with either 3D space plus 1D time, or 4D spacetime. Baumgarten doesn’t. With this generic model in hand, Baumgarten then makes a single assumption. He assumes that there exists at least one function of all those variables that remains constant in time. At least one conserved quantity. It doesn’t matter what it is, what it represents, etc. We don’t have to have it explicitly in hand - we merely need to assume that at least one - any one - exists. From there he simply draws out the consequences of this assumption. And the results are profound. “Physics” pours out. At one step he linearizes his model, so the results don’t cover all of physics, but they do cover all of low energy physics. Basic mechanics, relativity, electromagnetism, and more - these relationships simply “appear” in the math, and we are completely free to label them as our familiar phenomena. Under that one assumption, it turns out that the model must behave in the way we see the world around us behave. Most importantly for this discussion, though, space emerges. Or, rather, patterns of dynamics that ideally fit behaviors in multi-dimensional space appear, and from there it’s easy to presume that space is simply the canvas upon which our senses have evolved to “map those behaviors onto.” We have to see the behaviors somehow, after all. Now we can discuss the number of spatial dimensions. It turns out the math breaks down unless that count is “right.” Not just any number of dimensions will do. One spatial dimension won’t do. Two won’t do. Three will - three is the smallest number of dimensions that is consistent with the model’s mathematics. There are higher dimension counts that will work as well - I believe the next one is eight spatial dimensions. He provides a formula for the ones that will work. So, the important point here is that reality itself, at its most basic level, does not have spatial dimensions. Space is not a “container” that was provided in advance in which everything somehow appears. Rather, it is a pattern of behaviors that emerge from the dynamics of the things that are real (those variables in that arbitrarily large collection, that simply vary in time). It could be that we see three dimensions simply because we evolved to map the dynamics onto a three dimensional canvas. It’s possible that we might have evolved to map the dynamics onto an eight dimensional canvas - who’s to say? The number of dimensions should not be thought of as a fundamental attribute of reality, but rather as just a feature of the way we perceive reality and organize those perceptions in our minds. Perhaps in some other star system or some other galaxy far away there are creatures who perceive the world as eight-dimensional. It’s important to remember, though, that we’d all be perceiving the same dynamics - the altered perception would not give any “new capabilities.” It’s all just different ways of looking at the same business. I cannot recommend Baumgarten’s paper highly enough. I think it’s an extremely under-appreciated contribution to the literature, as are other papers of his. He’s clearly a deeply insightful mind. As a final note, I’ll say that Baumgarten’s approach - not assuming spatial dimensions as “a priori” things but rather allowing them to emerge naturally - seems to enable some insights that are hard to otherwise get. For example, you begin to see connections between classical and quantum mechanics that no one else talks about. It’s normally said that it’s impossible to get at quantum theory starting with a classical analysis - it’s why quantum theory is normally presented using a set of initial postulates. But Baumgarten does achieve insight into quantum physics using classical methods. That’s what motivated the title of the paper. Absolutely, totally worth the read. Worth several reads. Stay safe and well! Kip ____________________ If you enjoy my answers, please consider supporting my work at Kip Ingram's Space.

Question: What are some laws in science and/or physics that are considered unbreakable or unchangeable? Why are they believed to be so?
Answer: These tend to be the major foundational laws. The first one that springs to mind for me is the second law of thermodynamics. There are various ways to state this law; I’ll go with one by Clausius: Many scientists regard this law as the single most fundamental law in physics. Then we come to “the great conservation principles”: These all derive via Noether’s theorem from some symmetry of spacetime (time translation invariance, space translation invariance, and rotational invariance, respectively). This business of symmetries is wildly important - a large portion of 20th century physics wound up being based on the consideration of more sophisticated symmetries of various sorts. The high level idea in such programs is referred to as “gauge invariance,” and the resulting theories are considered “gauge theories.” Our simplest gauge theory is classical electromagnetism. We did not use gauge principles to obtain it, though - Maxwell worked it out before we knew about gauge ideas. Then we later recognized it as a gauge theory. But the Standard Model is largely based on gauge principles. General relativity is also a sort of gauge theory. A feature of the modern physics landscape that bothers me very much is the extent to which some people try to argue against these great conservation laws. There is in particular an active presence online that argues against the conservation of angular momentum. These people have somehow just chosen to delude themselves - I don’t know how they’ve gotten there, but please don’t waste your time and energy listening to them. Stay safe and well! Question: Are there alternative solutions to the measurement problem in quantum mechanics besides decoherence theory?
Answer: There’s not really a problem. The theory says very clearly what’s up. Nature is non-deterministic. Therefore, measurement outcomes cannot be predicted. However, the statistics of measurements can be predicted, and the program tells us very clearly what happens to the quantum system - how to modify its state after you have done your measurement and gotten your result. So, what’s bothering people is not really an issue with how to employ the paradigm. People are just bothered that the whole business doesn’t “sit with their intuition” as cleanly as they’d like for it to. People agitate over “what is a measurement.” The truth, though, is that you decide what a measurement is when you set up your problem. When you do that, one of the first decisions you make is what your quantum state is going to look like, explicitly. This will always have the general form of a) the detailed state of your “subsystem being measured” and b) the state of your instrument. For example, it might look something like this for an electron spin measurement: psi = (a*|electron spin up> + b*|electron spin down>)*|instrument ready> The next step is to make the measurement. This is tantamount to entangling the two parts of your state - you will now have something like psi = c*|electron spin up>*|instrument reads up> + d*|electron spin down>*|instrument reads down> Then finally you read off the result, and that directs you to discard one of these terms. This state, in all steps, has the general form |psi_electron>*|psi_instrument>. What you have to recognize is that these are very, very different sorts of things. Your psi_electron part will be fully detailed - capturing the entire relevant quantum state of the electron. But your psi_instrument is absolutely not capturing a fully detailed quantum state for the instrument. That instrument might have Avogadro’s number of quantum degrees of freedom, and you certainly are not including all of those in your state. So, what is a measurement? It is the process of entangling your fully detailed subsystem with your coarse, not detailed instrument state. You just decided what that was going to be when you designed the problem. You might argue that you can imagine writing down the whole state of the instrument. That’s true - you can imagine it, even though you can never do it in practice. But if you do that, then you have a problem. You have not provided a call-out of what you’re measuring. The theory requires you to do that. In that sense the theory is not really a theory about what’s going to happen in the world - it’s a theory about what you should expect re: your measurement results. If this bothers you I’m sorry, but you really can’t just insist that a theory is failing because it’s not the theory you want it...

Question: Nathan Coppedge. If you have been reading my recent posts, a quantum computer is a perpetual motion machine with circular algebra. It runs on heat, ejects heat and generates heat and can reuse that heat to run itself?
Answer: Let’s clear one thing up first. There is no law of physics that prohibits a process from being cyclic, and in the absence of all loss mechanisms a cyclic process will run forever. So, strictly speaking, that is a “perpetual motion machine.” The easiest to point to example of such a cyclic process is Earth turning on its axis, or orbiting the sun. Those processes have been coasting along on sheer inertia for four billion years, and will continue for more or less that much longer. If you want to be pedantic, it’s not “perpetual” - the gravitational stresses created by the moon move around inside Earth as it turns, and this causes small motions and thus small losses. I.e., there is a (very small) loss mechanism, so Earth will gradually slow down. This will continue until Earth’s rotation slows down to match the moon’s orbital period, and Earth will present the same face to the moon all the time. That will bring those internal changes to a halt, and the losses will cease. But in any case, in a few billion years the Sun will swell up into red giant status, and engulf Earth. So… not perpetual. But hopefully you can see what I am talking about here. There is no problem in physics with a process that repeats exactly over and over. The only reason we can build “every day life” machines that will run forever is that we just can’t get rid of all the losses. But… this isn’t what most people mean when they talk about “perpetual motion machines.” They use that phrase as a euphemism for a “free energy machine” - a system that they can draw energy off of, forever, without the energy ever running out. The solution to all the world’s ills - the dream machine. This most certainly is prohibited by physics. In a quantum computer you probably can create actual computation processes that don’t consume any energy. But, those processes do build up “waste results” (which is the quantum computing equivalent of entropy increase), and eventually you run out of any way to hold those results and you have to “erase” them. That consumes energy. It’s just like thermodynamics - the only way to drive entropy down in a system is to invest energy in doing that. And meanwhile you just eject that entropy somewhere else - you can never truly get rid of it. Don’t forget, though, that the quantum computers we’ve built so far have to be chilled to low temperatures, and that takes energy, and a lot of it. We are nowhere close to having some kind of “energy free computing paradigm.” Stay safe and well! Question: Why does time appear to slow down when moving at high speeds, but not when moving at slower speeds or walking normally?
Answer: It’s still slowing down - it just slows down way too little for you to notice. It’s a little like, “Why does water look smooth and continuous, when we all know it’s made of molecules?” The molecules are just far too small for you to see. Way, way too small. Similarly, the slow-down factor depends on speed like this: factor = sqrt(1-v^2/c^2) So let’s say your friend drives by you in his sports car at 150 miles per hour (probably one of the fastest relative motions you’d be seeing around you day to day). 150 mph is equal to right at 67 meters/sec. So that is our v. Meanwhile, c is 3e8 meters/sec (that’s 300000000 meters per second). Putting v and c into the expression above gives us factor = sqrt(1–67^2/3e8^2) = 0.99999999999975 See? You wouldn’t be able to tell that it wasn’t exactly 1.0, or “no slowdown.” On the other hand, let’s put in 75% of the speed of light. That gives us factor = sqrt(1–2.25e8^2/3e8^2) = 0.6614 and you would easily notice that if you’d arranged things so that you could actually see what was happening. The short answer is “the speed of light is really, really fast.” This same general kind of thing is why you don’t see strange quantum effects around you in the world, too. They’re happening all the time, in all the molecular processes around you. But there are so many of those molecular processes, and the weird stuff has a randomness to it, so it all tends to “average out” and the world seems to behave in a very sharp and precise way as far as you’re concerned. Question: What is the reason for time passing more slowly for objects in motion compared to stationary ones? Is it due to experiencing less time or is the exact cause unknown?
Answer: Well, it is a necessary consequence of the invariance of the laws of physics under relative motion. In other words, I can run experiments and use them to determine the laws of physics. You can do that too, and even if you are moving relative to me you will arrive at exactly the same laws. This invariance implies the existence of a “special speed” - an object moving at this speed will be measured as exactly the same by all observers regardless of their own state of motion. In our universe this is the speed we call the speed of light. Note that light has nothing to do with this really - the speed isn’t special “because it’s the speed of light.” Rather, it’s the other way around. Light quanta (photons) have no mass, and therefore they must travel at the “special speed.” Anyway, that universal agreement on things moving at the special speed forces the relativistic behavior of distances and times onto us - it must be the case that objects in motion will appear to shorten along the direction of motion and also appear to have time passing more slowly for themselves. As far as “why the laws of physics are invariant,” well, I think that’s where we get to “they just are” - we’ve learned that they are by observing the world. Physics doesn’t really promise us any “why” answers - it just tells us how the world behaves. Stay safe and well!
